Castle Roads: Riding Through British History

Britain has more castles per square mile than almost anywhere on Earth. From ruined Highland fortresses to imposing Welsh strongholds, these stone giants sit on dramatic landscapes that happen to be connected by some of the country's finest motorcycle roads. Here are the routes that combine great riding with castle-hopping.

Scotland's Castle Trail

Scotland's northeast has a designated Castle Trail with seventeen castles within easy riding distance:

  • Dunnottar Castle, Stonehaven: Perched on a dramatic clifftop, this ruined medieval fortress is one of Scotland's most photogenic. The A92 coastal road to reach it is excellent riding.
  • Craigievar Castle: The pink-toned tower house that supposedly inspired Walt Disney's castle logo. In rolling Aberdeenshire countryside.
  • Kilchurn Castle, Loch Awe: A ruined castle on a promontory jutting into Loch Awe. The A85 past here is a beautiful road through Argyll.
  • Eilean Donan Castle: Scotland's most photographed castle, at the meeting of three lochs on the road to Skye. The A87 ride to reach it through Glen Shiel is magnificent.
  • Urquhart Castle, Loch Ness: Overlooking Loch Ness from a rocky promontory. Best approached via the B862 south shore road.

Wales's Iron Ring

Edward I's ring of castles built to subdue Wales created an accidental motorcycle route of extraordinary quality:

  • Caernarfon Castle: The grandest of Edward's castles, dominating the Menai Strait. A UNESCO World Heritage Site.
  • Conwy Castle: Impressive walled town on the North Wales coast. The road into Conwy gives dramatic first views of the castle walls.
  • Harlech Castle: Set high above Cardigan Bay on a rocky promontory. The A496 coastal approach is stunning.
  • Beaumaris Castle: On Anglesey, the last and most technically perfect of Edward's castles. Cross the Menai Strait for a short detour to this geometric masterpiece.
  • Castell y Bere: A ruined native Welsh castle in the Dysynni Valley. The approach road through the valley is narrow, quiet, and beautiful.

England's Fortress Roads

  • Bamburgh Castle, Northumberland: A dramatic fortress overlooking miles of golden beach. The coastal B1340/B1341 roads leading here are among the finest in northeast England.
  • Dunstanburgh Castle: A ruined clifftop castle accessible only on foot from the road, but visible for miles from the coastal road. Park in Craster and walk 30 minutes across fields.
  • Corfe Castle, Dorset: An iconic ruin on the Purbeck Hills. The A351 through the Purbeck countryside is an excellent biking road.
  • Tintagel Castle, Cornwall: Legendary seat of King Arthur on the wild north Cornish coast. The B3263 approach drops dramatically to the coast.
Castles tell the story of the landscape. They're positioned on strategic heights, at river crossings, and on coastlines — the same features that create great motorcycle roads. Following the castles is following the geography that makes riding special.

Planning a Castle Tour

  • Many castles charge entry (£8-20). Historic Scotland and English Heritage annual passes pay for themselves after 3-4 visits.
  • Castles are often visible and photogenic from the road — you don't always need to pay to enter.
  • Allow 1-2 hours per castle if entering, or 15 minutes for a photo stop from outside.
  • Motorcycle parking is usually available and often free at historic sites.
  • Combine 3-4 castles in a day ride for a themed route with purpose and variety.

A castle tour adds history, culture, and a sense of journey to your motorcycle ride. These ancient stones have seen a thousand years of history — riding past them connects you to a story that stretches far beyond a single day's touring. keyTakeaways: Scotland's northeast Castle Trail links seventeen castles, including clifftop Dunnottar and Disney-inspiring Craigievar.
Edward I's Iron Ring of Welsh castles (Caernarfon, Conwy, Harlech, Beaumaris) forms an accidental world-class riding route.
Eilean Donan on the A87 is Scotland's most photographed castle, at the meeting of three lochs.
Many castles are photogenic from the road, so you do not always need to pay to enter.
Historic Scotland and English Heritage annual passes pay for themselves after three or four visits.

faq.q: Do I have to pay to enjoy these castles on a ride?
faq.a: Not at all. Many of the finest, including Dunnottar, Eilean Donan, Harlech, and Corfe, are strikingly photogenic from the road or a nearby lay-by, so a 15-minute photo stop costs nothing. Entry fees typically run 8 to 20 pounds if you want to go inside. Frequent visitors save money with a Historic Scotland or English Heritage membership.

faq.q: How many castles can I sensibly visit in a day?
faq.a: Three or four makes a satisfying themed ride without feeling rushed. Allow one to two hours per castle if you go inside, or about 15 minutes for an external photo stop. Combining, say, Bamburgh and Dunstanburgh on the Northumberland coast, or several of the Welsh Iron Ring, gives a day with history, variety, and excellent roads between stops.

faq.q: Is there motorcycle parking at these sites?
faq.a: Most historic attractions provide parking, and motorcycle spaces are often free even where cars pay. At popular sites like Caernarfon and Bamburgh, arrive earlier in the day to secure a sensible spot. For clifftop ruins reached on foot, such as Dunstanburgh from Craster, park in the village car park and walk the final 30 minutes across the fields.

faq.q: Which castle route is best for dramatic coastal riding?
faq.a: The Northumberland coast is hard to beat: the B1340 and B1341 link Bamburgh and Dunstanburgh past miles of golden sand with the Farne Islands offshore. In Scotland, the A92 to clifftop Dunnottar is superb, and in Wales the A496 coastal approach to Harlech is stunning. Each pairs great tarmac with fortresses positioned for maximum drama.
